8:35 When I get a poor night's sleep, I usually don't know it until the late afternoon when I finally crash. Hard. So sleep trackers have helped me prepare for my day, take it easy on tasks, more breaks, and set aside time in the afternoon for a gentle rest rather than unexpectedly pulling over into a parking lot to nap unrestfully.

PS it turns out I have chronic fatigue, so my baseline morning is pretty low energy, and subtle sleep changes have bigger effects for me. I think another reason I don't know right away about a poor night's sleep is that my body often kicks in some adrenaline in poor sleep mornings to get my basic needs met, so paradoxically feeling good and energetic in the morning is a warning sign for poor sleep for me and an impending crash.

Point is, the sleep trackers can be very helpful. Not everyone "just knows". Especially in a world where children are woken for school arbitrarily early and trained to ignore their body cues.

And after I used a tracker for a few years, I stopped because I've learned enough about my body cues (and how to wake up without an alarm, without adrenaline) to no longer warrant the effort of tracking.

comments.text: 13:08 In my late teens, I had a routine CBC panel that unexpectedly showed I was significantly anemic to the point that the doctor made me go to the hospital to get a two unit transfusion as soon as possible. Previous to that, I used to give blood regularly (I’m O- and I have my 1 gallon keychain ☺️) and I had told my doctor that I’d given a double unit of packed RBCs an entire three months prior. I guess I was never able to replenish what I had given, so they sent me to the cancer center to look into that. Turned out to be a massive peptic ulcer that was slowly leaking blood at about the same rate that my body would make it 😰 After my transfusion, the ulcer was treated, and I don’t think I’ve struggled with anemia since. Anemia in young people, like I was at the time, is definitely a red flag that needs looking into.
